How to shadow box for beginners

By the Box AI team · Updated November 5, 2026

Shadow boxing means throwing punches and moving as if you're boxing, with no opponent or equipment. To start, get into your stance, throw one punch at a time slowly, return your hands to your face after each one, and move your feet between punches. Begin with short rounds and add speed last.

How to shadow box, step by step

  1. Set your stance. Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and staggered, your weight on the balls of your feet, your elbows tucked and your chin down.
  2. Throw straight punches. Start with the jab and the cross. Aim at one spot, such as your own chin in a mirror, and rotate your rear hip and shoulder through the cross.
  3. Bring your hands back. Return each hand straight to your face before you do anything else. This habit matters more than speed.
  4. Move your feet. When one foot moves, the other follows the same distance. Step, then punch, then step again, without crossing your feet.
  5. Add defense. Slip or roll after your combinations, so you practice defending as well as attacking.

Stance and footwork points are adapted from FightCamp's shadow boxing guide, which also recommends a mirror and starting slowly.

A 15-minute shadow boxing routine

Do this at home, three times a week, with a boxing round timer. Each round lasts two minutes, with one minute of rest.

RoundWhat to doThink about
Warm-up2 minutes of easy movement, arm circles and light bouncingLoose shoulders
1Footwork only, with your guard upFeet never cross
2Jab, moving aroundHand straight back to your chin
31-2, jab then crossRotate your rear hip
41-2-3, adding the lead hookRear hand stays on your cheek
5Freestyle, with a slip after each comboStay relaxed and keep breathing

Shadow boxing combos for beginners

Boxers number punches: 1 jab, 2 cross, 3 lead hook, 4 rear hook, 5 lead uppercut, 6 rear uppercut. Start with these:

  • 1-1-2: double jab, cross
  • 1-2-3: jab, cross, lead hook
  • 1-2, slip, 2: jab, cross, slip, cross
  • 1-6-3: jab, rear uppercut, lead hook

Common shadow boxing mistakes

  • Dropping your hands. This is the most common one, and it gets worse as you tire. Film a round from the front to check. ExpertBoxing points to leaning back as a cause, so keep your weight slightly forward with your chin tucked.
  • Standing still. Move your feet between combinations, not only your arms.
  • Going too fast. Speed hides sloppy form. Slow down until each punch is clean.
  • Holding your breath. Breathe out sharply with each punch, and stay loose between them.
  • Overextending your elbow. Don't snap your arm to a hard lockout with nothing to hit. Keep your punches controlled.
  • Only attacking. Mix a slip or a roll into every combination.

Questions about shadow boxing

How long should a beginner shadow box?

Start with three to five rounds of two minutes each, with one minute of rest, for about 15 minutes in total. Add rounds or move to three-minute rounds once that feels comfortable.

Is shadow boxing a good workout?

Yes. It raises your heart rate and works your shoulders, core and legs with no equipment. The harder you work your feet and the shorter your rest, the more conditioning you get.

Can shadow boxing help you lose weight?

It can help as part of regular exercise, since it burns energy like other cardio. Weight loss depends on your overall activity and diet, so don't expect shadow boxing alone to do it.

Should you shadow box with hand weights?

Not as a beginner. Added weight can pull your form apart and put strain on your shoulders and elbows. Get your technique right first, and build strength separately.

Can you learn to box just by shadow boxing?

You can learn your stance, punches, footwork and basic defense from shadow boxing. You'll need a bag or pads to feel contact, and a live partner to learn timing. Read more in can you learn boxing at home?
